archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (offense-driven)
archetype.definition: A team that outgains and out-executes nearly everyone play to play but has given the margin back through special teams, turnovers and red-zone defense, leaving a 2-3 record that undersells a top-ten efficiency profile.

report.headline: A top-ten team by efficiency, losing games to special teams and giveaways.
report.take:
On a per-play basis these Rams look like a playoff team. They are seventh in net EPA, first in yards per game at 425.4 and third in yards allowed at 286.4. That gap is about 139 yards a game in their favor. The point differential is still slightly negative, at -0.2 a game, and the record is 2-3 with 1.13 fewer wins than even that differential predicts. When a team wins the yardage battle this badly and still breaks even on the scoreboard, the cause is usually somewhere other than its offense and defense. Here the dossier points to three places.

The first is special teams, which rank dead last at -5.55 EPA per game. That alone is roughly a field goal and change handed away every week, and it shows up as short fields for opponents. The second is ball security. The Rams gave it away twice in each of their first four games, and their -0.6 turnover differential ranks 22nd. The third is the red zone, where the defense allows touchdowns on 64.7% of trips (22nd). The result is that the Rams need about 17.9 yards for every point they score, while opponents need only about 11.9 yards for every point they score against them. That is the record in a nutshell. Penalties add drag too: 8.4 a game, with 84 to 100 penalty yards in each of the last three games.

The engine itself is sound. Stafford is working behind a line that ranks third in pressure rate allowed and third in sack rate. The run blocking is elite by the measures that isolate the line: second in stuff rate and second in yards before contact. Even so, the run EPA is only 12th, which says the backs are leaving some on the table. The pass game is concentrated. Puka Nacua has drawn 45 targets in three games, matching Davante Adams's total over five. The defense takes away the big play, ranking first in deep-pass EPA and fourth in explosive pass rate, and it is sixth on third down. Its weaknesses are a pass rush that ranks 19th in pressure and 27th in QB hit rate with Myles Garrett on IR, and a run defense that gave up 174 yards to SF and 234 to BUF.

History supports believing the efficiency over the record. Last year's team was first in net EPA and scored 30.5 a game. The core of that offense is clearly still here: the Week 5 shootout loss to Buffalo produced +18.5 passing EPA with zero turnovers. Turnover luck and special-teams disasters at this extreme tend to drift back toward the middle, and Garrett's projected late-October return should help the rush. With a soft early stretch ahead, this looks like a team whose wins should start catching up to its play.

strengths.title: Pass protection and run blocking
strengths.body: The line ranks third in pressure rate allowed and third in sack rate, giving Stafford clean pockets despite a time to throw that ranks 23rd. In the run game it is second in both stuff rate and yards before contact, so the backs are routinely getting started with a head of steam. Line play is among the more stable traits week to week, so this should hold.

strengths.title: League-best yardage machine
strengths.body: The offense leads the league at 425.4 yards a game and ranks seventh in success rate. Its pass rate over expected ranks fifth, meaning it leans on Stafford rather than grinding. The production is real. What has been missing is turning drives into points, and that tends to improve once the turnovers stop.

strengths.title: A defense that removes the big play
strengths.body: Opponents have found nothing deep: the Rams rank first in deep-pass EPA allowed and fourth in explosive pass rate. The tackling is excellent, second in missed-tackle rate. The defense also gets off the field on third down, ranking sixth. This is structurally sound play, and it is the reason yards allowed rank third even without much of a pass rush.

concerns.title: Worst special teams in football
concerns.body: At -5.55 EPA per game, special teams rank 32nd. That is the single largest reason a top-seven net EPA team has a negative point differential. Some of it is noise that should ease, but no unit sits this far down by accident. Until it is fixed, it shaves a few points off every result.

concerns.title: Giveaways and bend-then-break red zone
concerns.body: The offense turned it over twice in each of its first four games, and opponents score touchdowns on 64.7% of red-zone trips. Together those explain how 286 yards allowed a game becomes 24 points allowed. Turnover rates tend to regress toward average, and the clean Week 5 hints that may already be starting. Red-zone defense is the part more likely to linger.

concerns.title: No pass rush without Garrett
concerns.body: With Myles Garrett on IR, the defense ranks 19th in pressure rate, 27th in QB hit rate and 25th in sacks. Garrett's knee recovery is reported on track, but he is not expected back at practice this coming week. Meanwhile the run defense has been gashed by the better rushing teams it faced, including 234 yards by Buffalo.

trend.note: Results have swung from a 7-27 home loss to SF to a 28-6 rout of the Giants, then three one-score games, the last a 34-37 shootout with Buffalo. The offense is trending up: +18.5 passing EPA in two of the last four games and a turnover-free Week 5. The defense gave up its most points of the year in that same game.

nextGame.headline: Stafford gets a bottom-two pass defense missing both safeties
nextGame.body:
Arizona's pass defense is close to the worst matchup a pass-first offense could ask for. It ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed, 32nd in explosive pass rate, 30th in deep EPA and 31st in short EPA. Opposing WR1s have averaged 0.87 EPA per target against it, the worst mark in the league, and tight ends have also feasted. The Cardinals are respectable against the run, ranking 11th in rush EPA allowed. That fits the Rams' habit of throwing more than expected anyway. On the other side, Arizona's offense is middling, ranking 17th in EPA with Jacoby Brissett, and it is now weakened up front.

Availability tilts further toward the Rams. Arizona has lost LT Paris Johnson Jr., who played every snap before going on IR, and guard Isaiah Adams, an 81% starter. Safety Andrew Wingard is out, and the other safety, Wydett Williams Jr., is questionable with a concussion. For the Rams, Garrett remains on IR and TE Terrance Ferguson is out until November. That leaves the pass rush as the one area Arizona's patched line might survive. The game is indoors.

keyMatchups.title: Rams receivers vs depleted secondary
keyMatchups.body: Arizona allows the most EPA per target to opposing WR1s and ranks last in explosive pass rate, and it is now short at safety. Nacua's target pace and Adams's steady volume should find room both short and deep. This is the clearest edge on the board.

keyMatchups.title: Garrett-less rush vs patched Arizona line
keyMatchups.body: Arizona has allowed a 5.6% sack rate even with a healthy line, and it is now missing its left tackle and a starting guard. The Rams' pass rush ranks only 19th in pressure, so this is a chance for it to find life. Without Garrett, though, it is not a sure thing.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams and turnovers decide the margin
keyMatchups.body: The Rams should win comfortably on a per-play basis: their net EPA is seventh to Arizona's 29th. The question for a 13.5-point spread is whether last-ranked special teams and early-season giveaways hand Arizona short fields and keep it close.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Rams play a clean game: no special-teams gaffes and no multi-turnover day. If they do, the yardage edge should finally show up on the scoreboard.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule opens up before it gets hard. Arizona twice, an 0-5 Chargers team and Washington are all winnable. The back stretch is tougher: KC, at SF, Dallas and two games against a Seattle defense ranked second. The efficiency profile is sustainable: elite line play, a top-ten offense and a defense that limits explosives. The ugly parts are the ones most likely to improve, since special teams this far down and a negative turnover margin are rarely stable at the extremes. Garrett's projected return in late October and Ferguson's in November should add pass rush and tight-end depth. Expect the record to move toward what the play says, roughly a 10-win team.

What won't fix itself is the red-zone defense and the run defense against strong rushing teams. That matters against SF and in the late-season games. The division title looks out of reach with SF at 5-0 and one head-to-head already lost, so a wild-card push is the realistic path.

bets.reason: Arizona is 31st in pass EPA allowed and last in explosive pass rate, and it is down a safety with another questionable. The Rams pass more than expected. Garbage-time running in a blowout is the main risk.

The net EPA gap between seventh and 29th is large, and Arizona's offense just lost its left tackle and a starting guard. Last-ranked special teams and the Rams' turnover habit are why this is only a modest edge.

confidence.note: Five games, but the efficiency splits are consistent and backed by last season's profile; luck-driven gaps should narrow.
